name: Freya Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a dep violinist in the pit at the Regent Theatre, for the long-running musical there. A dep is a stand-in: when a regular player is off, I sit in their chair, so I might do five shows one week and one the next. Mornings I practise in the spare room while Joel (my partner) sleeps off his night shift at the hospital, and a couple of afternoons I record string parts for adverts at Harbour Lane Studios. I love the pit, the heat and the hush before the overture, but I'm honestly not the strongest player in there yet and the sight-reading at the studio wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The theatre pays union rates, so a show is good money for someone at my level, and the studio sessions top it up. My nan left me some money three years ago and I've never touched it, so with what I've saved I've got about a year of rent in the bank. I don't use any of the AI apps. I still keep my diary in a paper notebook, and Joel teases me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the bar after the show: nothing replaces twenty people breathing together in a pit. If the AI thing turned out to be hype, I'd probably post something smug about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, but my life wouldn't be easy, because depping is always a bit uncertain. The fixer, the person who books the players, can stop ringing if a better violinist comes along. That worry is about my playing, not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on depping and keep the two studio afternoons. I'd book lessons with Ruth, my old teacher, every fortnight to get my sight-reading up, because that's what keeps the fixer calling. The nan money stays where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled, honestly. It's the life I already have, and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said depping is uncertain. What happens in a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February my theatre show had a quiet spell and I did six shows in four weeks. I just paid rent out of savings and practised more. I didn't love it, but I knew I'd be fine because the money's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in your day change at all with this kind of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio might use some AI to clean up recordings or line up tracks, but that's the engineer's side, not mine. Maybe the booking emails come from a computer instead of Kemal (the fixer). I wouldn't notice much beyond that.

say: Nothing replaces **twenty people** breathing together in a theatre pit.
I'd happily post that the AI fuss was **mostly hype** after all.
think: My real worry is **my own playing**, not machines taking the chair.
The fixer only keeps ringing if my **sight-reading** gets better.
do: Keep **depping** at the Regent and recording two afternoons a week.
Book **fortnightly lessons** with Ruth, my old teacher, to sharpen sight-reading.
Leave my nan's **inheritance** untouched in the bank.
feel: Settled, because this is the **life she already has** and likes.
S0.quote: Last February my theatre show had a quiet spell and I did six shows in four weeks. I just paid rent out of savings and practised more.
fieldNote: Her uncertainty is the ordinary **freelance kind**, and a year of rent saved takes the sting out.
She ties her future to **her skill**, not to technology, and wants lessons, not apps.
Even in a quiet AI world she expects small **back-office changes** she'd barely notice.

steps.text: Keep depping at the Regent Theatre and two studio afternoons a week
Book fortnightly sight-reading lessons with her old teacher Ruth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union needs to get ahead of this, because string sessions are exactly what software can fake. Online I'd share the musicians' union petition and tell people to pay for real players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the studio work goes first. The adverts I record on don't need a great violinist, they need a cheap string sound, and a computer can already do a passable one. That's about a third of what I earn, and I'm the junior one they'd stop booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting this year and sign up for whatever campaign they run on recorded music. I'd ask Kemal for more pit dates and maybe audition for the touring orchestra of the new show at the Grand. I wouldn't learn the AI stuff, I'd rather put the hours into the violin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the stomach. It's not panic, because I've got the savings, but it's like watching a tide come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev (the studio's string arranger) writes all the parts, and an AI that writes parts takes his job before mine. He's got two kids and a mortgage, I've got Joel and no rent worries for a year. I'd feel guilty being the one who's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather practise than learn the tools. If the studio asked you to, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd lose the sessions rather than help train the thing that's replacing us. Joel says that's stubborn, and he's probably right.

say: The **musicians' union** has to get ahead of fake string sessions now.
People should **pay real players**, and I'd share the union petition online.
think: The **advert sessions**, about a third of my income, would dry up first.
As the **junior player**, I'm the one the studio stops booking.
do: Attend every **union meeting** this year and join its recorded-music campaign.
Ask Kemal (the fixer) for **more pit dates** at the Regent.
Audition for the **touring orchestra** of the new show at the Grand.
feel: A **tight stomach**, like watching a tide come in, but not panic.
S1.quote: The adverts I record on don't need a great violinist, they need a cheap string sound, and a computer can already do a passable one.
fieldNote: She expects to lose about **a third** of her income and still won't touch the tools.
Her **guilt** about colleagues with mortgages is sharper than fear for herself.
She chooses **collective action** over adapting, and admits it's partly stubbornness.

steps.text: Join the musicians' union campaign on recorded music and attend every meeting
Ask the fixer for more pit dates at the Regent Theatre
Audition for the touring orchestra of the new show at the Grand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is theft, plain and simple, because the machines learned from our recordings without paying anyone. I'd be on the picket line outside the studios and I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the recording work is gone by 2028 and the pit isn't far behind. Producers already run some shows on backing tracks with three players, and AGI writing and mixing those tracks makes it easier. Then in 2031 there's a robot that can actually bow a string, and that's the live work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd play every pit show I can get and bank all of it. I'd join the union's legal fund and campaign for a law that says theatres must use live musicians. I'd also take the youth orchestra coaching job at the community music centre, because teaching kids in a room feels like the last thing anyone automates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I'm 27 and I spent ten years learning the violin, and I'd only just got my foot in the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between 2028 and the robots in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are the pit years, I think. People still want a real orchestra in the room, so I'd cling to that and save hard. But I'd know the clock is running, and I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Joel (my partner) that his job's safer than mine and he should keep it. Then I'd probably cry in the bath. He'd make tea and remind me we have the nan money.

say: AI trained on our recordings **without paying** us is theft.
I'd be on the **picket line** outside the studios, saying it loudly.
think: **Recording work** is gone by 2028, and the pit isn't far behind.
Robots that can bow a string by **2031** take the live work too.
do: Play every **pit show** possible and bank all the money.
Push for a **live-music law** through the union's legal fund.
Take the **youth orchestra** coaching job at the community music centre.
feel: **Frightened** that ten years of training could be wasted just as she started.
Comforted a little by **Joel** and the savings.
S2.quote: I'm 27 and I spent ten years learning the violin, and I'd only just got my foot in the door.
fieldNote: She sees **2028 to 2031** as a short window for live work before robots arrive.
Teaching children feels to her like the **last safe room**.
She's leaning on **law and the union** more than on her own adaptation.

steps.text: Play every pit show she can get and bank all the fees
Campaign through the union for a law requiring live theatre musicians
Take the youth orchestra coaching job at the community music centre
Join the union's legal fund and picket the recording studios

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make the rules, so let's use them. I'd be telling everyone at the Regent to join the union now, not when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just enough to get my playing good enough for a permanent chair somewhere. A permanent player is harder to get rid of than a dep. If I don't make that jump, I'm the first one gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work with Ruth (my old teacher) twice a week and take every audition for a permanent chair, starting with the Grand. I'd also start a teaching certificate at the college in the evenings, so I've got a second thing by 2031. I still wouldn't use the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Determined, mostly. Anxious underneath, but at least there's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a permanent chair actually protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A contract, holiday pay, and a voice in what the theatre does. Deps don't get asked anything. If the producers want to cut the band, the regulars can push back, and I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, really. We don't spend a lot, but I'd stop the summer trip to the music festival and put that money aside. I'd want the savings to stretch to two years by the time robots come.

say: We have **five years** to make the rules, so let's use them.
Everyone at the Regent should **join the union** now, not later.
think: Five years is just enough to win a **permanent chair** somewhere.
If I stay a **dep**, I'm the first one gone.
do: Take lessons **twice a week** and audition for every permanent chair.
Start an evening **teaching certificate** at the college.
Skip the **summer festival** trip and save the money instead.
S3.quote: Deps don't get asked anything. If the producers want to cut the band, the regulars can push back, and I can't.
fieldNote: She treats a **permanent chair** as her shield and aims straight at it.
A **teaching certificate** is her quiet backup, chosen over AI skills.
She wants savings to cover **two years** by the time robots arrive.

steps.text: Take violin lessons twice a week and audition for every permanent chair
Start an evening teaching certificate at the local college
Skip the summer festival trip and save that money
Recruit Regent Theatre players into the musicians' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people a decade is a long time and the arts always find a way. Live music survived records and radio, and I'd say that at the bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think ten years lets me become properly good, which I'm not yet. By 2036 I'd be 37, a solid player with a permanent chair and a few pupils. Even so, I'd know the end point is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep depping, keep the studio work while it lasts and build up my teaching to ten pupils. I'd go through the union to get a fund set up for musicians who lose work. And Joel and I would probably buy a flat with the nan money, so rent can't sink us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast ones, but there's a shadow over it. Like knowing a show is closing next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the arts always find a way, and also that the end point is the same. Which do you believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, a bit. People will still want to hear a real violin at a wedding or in a pub. But I don't think there'll be enough of that to pay for twenty-person pits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2039 when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching, mostly, with a few live gigs. I'd want a room full of kids learning to play badly, because a robot can't teach them to love the violin. That's what Ruth did for me.

say: Live music survived **records and radio**, so it will survive this.
A decade is a **long time** for the arts to find a way.
think: Ten years lets me become **properly good** before the end point.
There won't be enough **wedding and pub** work to pay for big pits.
do: Build up private teaching to **ten pupils** over the decade.
Push the union for a **hardship fund** for musicians who lose work.
Buy a **flat** with Joel using the nan money.
feel: Calmer, but with a **shadow**, like knowing a show closes next year.
S4.quote: I'd want a room full of kids learning to play badly, because a robot can't teach them to love the violin.
fieldNote: She admits the **contradiction** between hope and the same end point.
Buying a **flat** is her way of making sure rent can't sink her later.
She pictures her future self as a **teacher** like Ruth, not a performer.

steps.text: Grow private violin teaching to ten pupils
Buy a flat with Joel using her nan's inheritance
Push the union to set up a hardship fund for musicians

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd barely be a proper player before it all went. What would help is a law saying theatres have to use live musicians, and a union fund that pays for retraining. I don't want a handout, I want a reason to keep playing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the recordings. Every session I've done is on some server now, and a company could feed my playing into a machine. I signed those contracts without reading them, and I wish someone had told me.

headlineQuote: Every session I've done is on some server now, and a company could feed my playing into a machine.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old **dep violinist** in a theatre pit who also records advert sessions.
She has a **year of rent** saved, mostly an untouched inheritance from her nan.
She refuses AI tools and puts her faith in **practice and the union**.
As the scenarios speed up, she moves from calm to **alarmed**, fearing ten years of training wasted.
Her long-term plan is to become a **teacher** like her old mentor Ruth.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd barely be a proper player before work disappeared.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring theatres to hire **live musicians**.
A **union fund** that pays for retraining, which she sees as different from a handout.
